items.note: The decision guide names CloudFront for lowest latency to web users and Global Accelerator for reliability, security, latency, gaming, IoT and VoIP. Route 53 and ELB are separated only by guide category (edge networking vs application networking); no sentence compares them, so none is quoted.

Link the S3 side from chapter 21: s3-faq-ta-vs-cloudfront, s3-transfer-acceleration-vs-cloudfront-small-objects. CloudFront FAQ lists PUT and POST among supported methods and says PUT/POST/PATCH/DELETE responses are not cached (proxied to the origin).

Hypothesis confirmed: origin fetch from AWS origins is free; GA adds DT-Premium on top of EC2 data transfer out. Dollar amounts of GA (hourly fee, DT-Premium table) are on the pricing page without a Region statement for the fixed fee, so no GA dollar amount was stored.

'When a CDN adds little': AWS does not say a CDN is useless for uncacheable APIs; it says CloudFront still shortens connection setup for dynamic uncacheable workloads. The weak fits that AWS names are Origin Shield for low-cacheability content and, for Global Accelerator versus a regional load balancer, a single-Region audience (faq lens fact).

Answer to Ana: no, the bucket does not have to be public; the page says content can be reached through the CloudFront distribution but not directly with S3 URLs. Accepted cost of caching (old files after a release): versioned names or invalidation.

TCP and UDP listeners, two static IPs, traffic dial 0 to drain a Region, unhealthy endpoint out in under one minute (FAQ). CloudFront serves HTTP streaming only, so live two-way audio is the Global Accelerator case.

Supercell edge-services page: only 'exploring' Global Accelerator, so no Global Accelerator quote; its CloudFront claims have no numbers. The Skyscanner Global Accelerator numbers in the GA FAQ are FAQ quotes.
FAQ: CloudFront Functions is meant to complement Lambda@Edge, not replace it. Confirmed by the comparison table.

Mapping: bucket only via CloudFront = OAC; paid subscribers only = signed URLs (single files) or signed cookies (many files); block a country = geographic restriction (whole distribution, country level); block bad IPs = AWS WAF web ACL.

contradictions_between_sources.topic: CloudFront Anycast static IPs and IPv6
contradictions_between_sources.detail: The CloudFront FAQ lists 'You must disable IPv6 when using Anycast Static IPs' among the exceptions while another answer on the same page says dual-stack is supported; the 2025-11-05 post and history row say IPv4 or dual-stack.
CloudFront flat-rate documentation says 750+ edge locations; the LadiPage customer story (2024) says over 600 points of presence. Edge counts are volatile; the numbers lens owns them.

History rows and What's New posts differ by one to twelve days (OAC 08-24 vs 08-25, cross-account VPC origins 11-05 vs 11-06, apex Anycast 04-04 vs 04-16, post-quantum 09-04 vs 09-05, stale directives 05-15 vs 05-17). Facts use the post date when the post is the evidence and the row date when the row is the evidence; both are in the claim or note.

Changes from 2026 (cache tag invalidation, origin mTLS, SHA-256, flat-rate API, MRAP OAC) appear only as What's New posts; the fetched 2025 and 2026 posts are quotable, the 2022 to 2024 posts are blocked by robots.txt, so those changes rest on history rows.
